message.content:
The sea was a greedy thing, licking the granite bones of the cliff with a white-toothed hunger. Elias, the keeper, knew its moods better than his own. Tonight, the wind was a howling thief, stealing the warmth from his bones as he climbed the spiral stairs, the heavy brass key cold in his hand.

His lantern was the only star in a sky drowned in ink. He fed it oil, coaxing the flame to life, and the great lens, a jewel of a thousand prisms, caught the light and flung it across the churning blackness. A single, defiant eye against the storm.

He thought of his wife, gone three years now, her memory as salt-stiff as the ropes that bound the buoys. He spoke to her sometimes, in the creak of the door, in the hiss of the lamp. "It's a wild one tonight, Mary," he muttered, his voice swallowed by the roar.

Then, a sound beneath the wind—not the sea, but a cry. Human. Thin and desperate. He grabbed his binoculars, scanning the foam-scoured rocks below. There—a flash of white, a tangled shape clinging to the wreck of a boat. A life, fighting for its own
